topic.name: Determining Characteristics of Moving Objects Using Differentiation

question.text: The displacement $s,$ in meters, relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t) = 3t^2 - 9t + 1$, where $t \gt 0$ is the time, measured in seconds. Find the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x.$
question.explanation:
If the particle moves in the direction of increasing $x,$ then its velocity is positive.

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

\begin{align} v(t) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}s}{\textrm{d}t} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left( 3t^2 - 9t + 1 \right) \\[5pt] & = 6t - 9 \end{align}

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x$, we solve $v(t) > 0\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align} v(t) &> 0\\[3pt] 6t - 9 &> 0\\[3pt] 6t & > 9\\[3pt] t & > \dfrac{3}{2} \end{align}

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of increasing $x$ is $t \in\left(\dfrac{3}{2} , \infty\right).$

example.title: Determining Intervals of Increasing or Decreasing Displacement

question.text: The displacement $s,$ in meters, relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t) = (3t + 1)e^{-t}$, where $t \geq 0$ is the time measured in seconds. Determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x.$
question.explanation:
If the particle moves in the direction of decreasing $x,$ then its velocity is negative.

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

\begin{align} v(t) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}s}{\textrm{d}t} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left( (3t + 1)e^{-t} \right) \\[5pt] & = (2 - 3t)e^{-t} \end{align}

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x$, we solve the inequality $v(t) < 0\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align} v(t) &< 0\\[3pt] (2 - 3t)e^{-t} &< 0\\[3pt] 2 - 3t &< 0\\[3pt] 3t & > 2\\[3pt] t & > \dfrac{2}{3} \end{align}

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of decreasing $x$ is $t\in\left( \dfrac{2}{3}, \infty\right).$

question.text: A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by \[ s(t) = t^2\ln(t) ,\quad t\geq 0. \] Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
question.explanation:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t)\mathbin{:}$

\[ \begin{align} v(t) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}s}{\textrm{d}t}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left( t^2\ln(t)\right)\\[5pt] &= 2t\ln (t) +t \end{align} \]

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t)\mathbin{:}$ \[ \begin{align} a(t) &=\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left( t +2t\ln (t) \right)\\[5pt] &= 2\ln (t) +3 \end{align} \]

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero: \[ \begin{align} 0 &= 2\ln (t) +3 \\[3pt] 2\ln (t) &= -3 \\[3pt] \ln (t) &= -\dfrac{3}{2} \\[3pt] t &= e^{-3/2} \end{align} \]

So the acceleration is zero when $t=e^{-3/2}.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get \begin{align*} v\left(e^{-3/2}\right) &= 2(e^{-3/2})\ln (e^{-3/2}) +e^{-3/2} \\[3pt] &= 2e^{-3/2}\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right) +e^{-3/2} \\[3pt] &= -2e^{-3/2}. \end{align*}
